systemsMapSummary: 1:1s are the first thing to fall out of a busy week, and three reinforcing loops explain why: nothing protects the slot, so a 1:1 loses every collision with delivery work; no one can see who is actually holding them, so there is no accountability and no norm; and managers who were never coached find them awkward and let them lapse. An unprotected slot, held by an unsure manager, that no one is watching, reliably disappears. Coverage sits at 38% even though 82% of managers say 1:1s matter.
headline: If we protected the slot, made cadence visible, and gave managers a simple structure to run, we'd likely see 1:1 coverage move from 38% toward the 80% target without adding a new tool.

topLeveragePoints.point: Protect the 1:1 as a recurring, hard-to-move calendar hold
topLeveragePoints.currentState: 1:1s sit in an already-full calendar with nothing defending the slot; ~45% of booked 1:1s are bumped or cancelled.

topLeveragePoints.point: Make holding 1:1s visible to managers and their leaders
topLeveragePoints.currentState: No one can see who is actually holding 1:1s, so there is no accountability and no norm.

topLeveragePoints.point: Give managers a simple, reusable 1:1 structure so it feels easy to run
topLeveragePoints.currentState: Managers who were never coached are unsure what to cover, so the meeting feels awkward and gets dropped.

topLeveragePoints.point: Have skip-level leaders ask about 1:1s in their own 1:1s
topLeveragePoints.currentState: Leaders rarely ask whether 1:1s are happening, so managers get no upstream signal that cadence matters.

topLeveragePoints.point: Default every new manager–report pair into a standing 1:1 at onboarding
topLeveragePoints.currentState: New pairs start with no 1:1 booked, so the slot has to be created by an already-busy manager.

behaviors.description: Skip-level leader asks their managers whether 1:1s are happening

Raises — or swallows — issues depending on whether the 1:1 happens
Signals whether 1:1s matter by asking about them, or not

causeEffect.note: The slot loses every collision with 'real work'
A single question upstream cues the behaviour

loops: Priority loop: unprotected slot -> 1:1 bumped -> weaker coaching habit -> 1:1 feels optional -> even easier to bump next time.
Visibility loop: no one sees cadence -> no accountability or norm -> fewer managers hold 1:1s -> even less of a visible norm to follow.

comb.barrier: Running a focused 30-minute conversation is physically undemanding; technique is not the limiting factor here.
Managers who were never coached are unsure what a 1:1 should cover, so they avoid what feels awkward.

comb.source: Manager pulse: '(I'm) not sure what a 1:1 should cover' common among newer managers

comb.barrier: There is no protected time — the 1:1 sits in a full calendar with nothing defending the slot, so it loses every collision with delivery work.

strongestBarriers.barrier: No protected time, so 1:1s lose every collision with delivery work
strongestBarriers.rationale: Highest impact and a defaults-and-friction problem: a recurring protected hold converts existing intent into a kept commitment without asking managers to care more.

strongestBarriers.barrier: Managers were never coached on how to run a 1:1, so they avoid what feels awkward
strongestBarriers.rationale: High impact and highly changeable; a light, reusable structure removes the 'what do I even say' friction that makes the meeting droppable.

strongestBarriers.barrier: Cadence is invisible, so there is no accountability or norm
strongestBarriers.rationale: Reinforces the other two: making cadence observable turns social proof from a headwind into a tailwind.

barrierNarratives.point: Protect the 1:1 as a recurring, hard-to-move calendar hold
barrierNarratives.narrative: The slot loses to delivery work because nothing defends it. A recurring, protected hold removes the weekly re-decision — it takes friction away rather than adding a rule, and it is the cheapest, most reversible lever.

barrierNarratives.point: Make holding 1:1s visible to managers and their leaders
barrierNarratives.narrative: What no one can see, no one sustains. Making cadence observable creates gentle accountability and a positive norm, so holding 1:1s stops depending on each manager's willpower alone.

barrierNarratives.point: Give managers a simple, reusable 1:1 structure so it feels easy to run
barrierNarratives.narrative: Managers drop what feels awkward. A simple, reusable structure lowers the skill barrier so an unsure manager can run a good-enough 1:1 without preparing from scratch each time.

gapLog.content: 'Held a 1:1' is self-reported in the engagement pulse, not instrumented — occurrence and quality are both unverified.
The ~45% bump rate from a two-team calendar sample generalises to all teams.
Confirm whether monthly 1:1s are a written manager expectation or only a cultural norm — ownership of enforcement is unclear.
There is no measure of 1:1 quality; a rushed status update and a real coaching conversation currently count the same.

discoveryActivities: 5-8 interviews with managers who rarely hold 1:1s to confirm whether time, skill, or priority is the real blocker.
A calendar audit across more teams to measure how often 1:1s are booked, kept, and bumped.
A short norms survey comparing how important managers say 1:1s are with how often they hold them.
Instrument a lightweight cadence signal (for example a recurring calendar tag) so coverage can be measured rather than self-reported.
